title: Visualizing the Structure of Plant Plasmodesmata with Cryo-ET
content: Cytoplasmic bridges across cell walls in plants which allow for communication and transport between adjacent cells are important structures in plant biology. These structures vary significantly in their dimensions, from large pores with diameters greater than 5um, down to channels 50nm diameter or less. Smaller channels are generally referred to as plasmodesmata and consist of a continuous extension of the endoplasmic reticulum between adjacent cells across the cell wall which is surrounded by a cytosolic sleeve and plasma membrane forming a channel across the cell wall [1]. Plasmodesmata in plants have been imaged previously with conventional plastic embedding and sectioning techniques, although inconsistency in negative staining and artifacts resulting from the embedding and sectioning process have led to ambiguities over the dimensional accuracy of proposed models and the interpretation of previous imaging using these conventional techniques [2]. Transport is generally assumed to occur through the cytosolic sleeve, although electron micrographs of resin embedded plasmodesmata often have cytosolic sleeve dimensions, particularly around the constricted neck region, which are less than the hydrodynamic volume of molecules with known diffusivity across the plasmodesmata of the plant tissue imaged [2]. Cryo-electron microscopy and tomography are ideal approaches for characterizing these structures free of artifacts, but difficulties with achieving thin, vitrified plant tissues containing plasmodesmata has so far limited results in this area. Here we show our efforts and results in cryogenic preparation of plant tissues, thin sectioning cell interfaces, and imaging individual plasmodesmata with cryo-electron tomography revealing their structure.
